title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch, with the same faintly solemn manner he used to wear when taking the chair at his board meetings, walked into Alexey Alexandrovitch's room. Alexey Alexandrovitch was pacing about with his hands behind his back, thinking about the very thing Stepan Arkadyevitch had just been discussing with his wife.

"I'm not interrupting?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who was suddenly conscious of an embarrassment unusual for him at the sight of his brother-in-law. To cover it he pulled out a cigarette case he had just bought, one that opened in a new way, and sniffed the leather before taking out a cigarette.
"No. Is there something you want?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked without warmth.
"Yes, I wished… I wanted… yes, I wanted to talk with you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, startled to find himself feeling an unfamiliar shyness.
The feeling was so unexpected and so strange that he refused to recognize it as the voice of conscience telling him that what he was about to do was wrong.
Stepan Arkadyevitch made an effort and pushed past the timidity that had come over him.
"I hope you believe in my love for my sister and in my sincere affection and respect for you," he said, reddening.
Alexey Alexandrovitch stood motionless and said nothing, but his face struck Stepan Arkadyevitch with its expression of unresisting sacrifice.
"I intended… I wanted to have a little talk with you about my sister and about your situation together," he said, still wrestling with that unaccustomed constraint.
Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled sadly, looked at his brother-in-law, and without answering walked over to the table, picked up an unfinished letter, and handed it to him.

"I think of nothing else. And here — this is what I had started to write, because I thought I could say it better in a letter, and because my presence irritates her," he said as he gave him the letter.
Stepan Arkadyevitch took it, glanced with incredulous surprise at the dull eyes fixed steadily on him, and began to read.

"I see that my presence is a burden to you. Painful as it is for me to believe it, I see that it is so and that it cannot be otherwise. I do not blame you, and God is my witness that, when I saw you during your illness, I resolved with my whole heart to forget all that had passed between us and to begin a new life. I do not regret, and never will regret, what I did; but I have wanted one thing — your good, the good of your soul — and now I see that I have failed to achieve it. Tell me yourself what will give you true happiness and peace of soul. I put myself entirely in your hands, and I trust your sense of what is right."

Stepan Arkadyevitch handed back the letter, and with the same surprise kept staring at his brother-in-law, not knowing what to say. The silence was so awkward for both of them that Stepan Arkadyevitch's lips began to twitch nervously as he went on gazing wordlessly at Karenin's face.
"That's what I wanted to say to her," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, turning away.
"Yes, yes…." said Stepan Arkadyevitch, unable to answer because of the tears choking him.
"Yes, yes, I understand you," he finally got out.
"I want to know what she would like," said Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"I'm afraid she doesn't understand her own position. She is not the right judge," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, recovering. "She is crushed — simply crushed by your generosity. If she read this letter, she wouldn't be able to say a word; she would only hang her head still lower."
"Yes, but what is to be done in that case? How can I explain — how find out what she wants?"
"If you'll allow me to give my opinion, I think it falls to you to spell out directly the steps you consider necessary to put an end to the situation."
"So you think it has to be ended?" Alexey Alexandrovitch interrupted him. "But how?" he added, lifting his hands before his eyes in a gesture not usual with him. "I see no way out."

"There is some way out of every situation," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, standing up and growing more cheerful. "There was a time when you considered breaking it off…. If you are now convinced that you cannot make each other happy…."
"Happiness can be defined in different ways. But suppose I agree to everything, that I want nothing — what way out of our situation is there then?"

"If you care to hear my opinion," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, with the same soothing, almond-oil smile he had used with Anna. His friendly smile was so winning that Alexey Alexandrovitch, conscious of his own weakness and unconsciously swayed by it, was ready to believe whatever Stepan Arkadyevitch was about to tell him.

"She will never say it. But there is one thing possible, one thing she might wish for," he went on, "and that is the end of your relationship and of all the memories tied to it. The way I see it, in your position what's needed is a new footing toward each other. And that can only stand on a foundation of freedom on both sides."
"Divorce," Alexey Alexandrovitch interrupted, in a tone of distaste.

"Yes, I suppose divorce — yes, divorce," Stepan Arkadyevitch repeated, reddening. "From every angle that is the most reasonable course for married people who find themselves in your situation. What else can be done if married people discover that life together has become impossible? That can always happen."
Alexey Alexandrovitch sighed heavily and closed his eyes.
"There's only one point to consider: does either of you want to form new ties? If not, the matter is very simple," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, his constraint slipping further away.

Alexey Alexandrovitch, scowling with emotion, muttered something to himself and gave no answer. What seemed so simple to Stepan Arkadyevitch, Alexey Alexandrovitch had thought through a thousand times. And so far from being simple, it all looked utterly impossible to him. Divorce, the details of which he knew by now, struck him as out of the question, because his sense of his own dignity and his respect for religion would not let him take on himself a fictitious accusation of adultery — still less let his wife, whom he had forgiven and still loved, be caught in the act and publicly disgraced. Divorce seemed impossible to him on other, weightier grounds as well.

What would become of his son in the event of a divorce? Leaving him with his mother was out of the question. The divorced mother would have her own illegitimate family, in which his position as a stepson and his upbringing would not be good. Keep him with himself? He knew that would be an act of revenge on his part, and he did not want that. But beyond all this, what made divorce most impossible of all to Alexey Alexandrovitch was that by agreeing to it he would be completely destroying Anna. Darya Alexandrovna's words in Moscow — that in deciding on a divorce he was thinking of himself, and not considering that by doing so he would be ruining her past saving — had sunk deep into him. And connecting that with his forgiveness of her and his devotion to the children, he understood it now in his own way. To consent to a divorce, to give her her freedom, meant in his mind to take from himself the last thing tying him to life — the children whom he loved; and to take from her the last support that held her on the path of right, pushing her down to her ruin. If she were divorced, he knew she would join her life to Vronsky's, and their union would be an unlawful, criminal one, since by the interpretation of church law a wife cannot marry while her husband is living. "She'll join him, and in a year or two he'll throw her over, or she'll form a new attachment," Alexey Alexandrovitch thought. "And I, by consenting to an unlawful divorce, will be to blame for her ruin." He had thought it all through hundreds of times, and was convinced that divorce was not at all simple, as Stepan Arkadyevitch had said, but utterly impossible. He didn't believe a single word Stepan Arkadyevitch was saying to him; to every word he had a thousand objections to raise, yet he kept listening, feeling that the words were the voice of that crude, overpowering force that ruled his life and to which he would have to submit.
"The only question is on what terms you would agree to give her a divorce. She wants nothing, she doesn't dare ask you for anything — she leaves it all to your generosity."

"My God, my God! Why?" thought Alexey Alexandrovitch, remembering the details of divorce proceedings in which the husband took the blame on himself, and with exactly the same gesture Vronsky had once made, he hid his face in his hands for shame.
"You're upset, I understand. But if you think it over…."
"Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also; and if any man take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also," thought Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"Yes, yes!" he cried in a shrill voice. "I'll take the disgrace on myself, I'll even give up my son, but… wouldn't it be better to leave it all alone? Still, do as you like…."

And turning away so his brother-in-law could not see him, he sat down on a chair by the window. There was bitterness in his heart, there was shame, but along with the bitterness and shame he felt a joy and a thrill at the height of his own meekness.
Stepan Arkadyevitch was touched. He stayed silent for a while.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch, believe me, she values your generosity," he said. "But it seems this was the will of God," he added, and as soon as he had said it he felt how foolish the remark was and barely kept from smiling at his own foolishness.
Alexey Alexandrovitch would have answered something, but tears stopped him.
"This is an unhappy fate, and one must accept it as such. I accept the calamity as a done thing and I'm doing what I can to help both her and you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.

When he left his brother-in-law's room he was moved, but that didn't prevent him from being pleased that he had brought the business to a satisfactory close, for he was certain that Alexey Alexandrovitch would not go back on his words. To this satisfaction was added the fact that an idea had just struck him for a riddle turning on his successful achievement — one he would ask his wife and his closest friends once the affair was finished. He turned the riddle over in two or three different forms. "But I'll polish it better than that," he said to himself with a smile.
